anchors.fact: After the 1906 earthquake and fire in San Francisco, several clergymen called the destruction divine retribution for the city's sins (Minnick 2024, F4).
anchors.meaning: The thing people were asked to swallow: that those who had just lost their city had deserved it.
anchors.speaksTo: the lie everyone pretends to believe; limb 1 (on the city's side, never against faith)

anchors.fact: The Hotaling whiskey warehouse survived, and people saved it: its own staff, with the fire department and the Navy (Minnick 2024, F5); its employees moved thousands of barrels to an empty lot (Wikipedia citing SF Heritage, F6).
anchors.speaksTo: Wren's condition 4; the whiskey is the punchline, never a miracle

anchors.fact: Charles K. Field, a journalist and poet, is credited with four lines (one version, V1): "If, as they say, God spanked the town / For being over frisky, / Why did He burn the churches down / And save Hotaling's whiskey?" (Minnick 2024; attributed to him in 1962 too, F8–F10).
anchors.meaning: The contradiction turned into a question; the joke does the arguing.
anchors.speaksTo: wit that tells the truth; what they give: the line that lets everyone breathe out

anchors.fact: The verse was still being retold more than a hundred years after the fire (Minnick 2024; also a 1962 *ABA Journal* essay, as Wikipedia quotes it; F11). Its own year is on no page (L6).
anchors.meaning: People kept the line. Never "the whole city", never "at once", never "in 1906" for the poem.

anchors.fact: Two decades after the fire, from 1927 to 1940, Field hosted *Cheerio* on NBC: poetry and inspirational talks (OAC Stanford M1533; Wikipedia, F12–F13).
anchors.meaning: The hope under the jibe, on record, in the same life.
anchors.speaksTo: the one true thing: a disappointed idealist who never stopped hoping; driver: seek paradise

anchors.fact: He went on air as "Cheerio", a made-up name; no press photographs were allowed, and his fee went to charity (OAC, F14; Wikipedia, F15). Passive on the page: who decided isn't recorded.
anchors.meaning: The hope went out nameless and faceless; the hope itself was broadcast, never hidden. His choosing it is "I like to think".
anchors.speaksTo: hides belief; position: the other way round, once

cocktail.closingLine: Take the peel away once its oil is on. Then, for once, say the hope first and the joke second.
cocktail.glassware: cocktail glass (about 180 ml), chilled, no ice
method: The night before, make the pear syrup. Stir the chopped pear and the sugar together in a jar, close it and leave it in the fridge overnight. In the morning, press it through a sieve and keep only the syrup. Keep it in a closed jar in the fridge and use it within a week. If it comes out thin, use 10 ml in the drink.
Put the cocktail glass in the freezer.
Pour the bourbon, the dry vermouth, the pear syrup and the bitters into a mixing glass or a jar.
Fill it with ice and stir with a long spoon for about 30 seconds, until the outside is very cold.
Hold the strip of lemon peel over the drink, shiny side down, and squeeze it so its oils fall on the surface. Then take it away.
cocktail.name: Against My Better Judgement

recipe.note: any straight bourbon, about 45%; no particular bottle
made the night before (below); the sweet part a sweet vermouth would usually give
squeezed over the top, then taken away: no garnish stays in the glass

recipe.item: *for the pear syrup:* 1 ripe pear (about 150 g peeled and cored), chopped small, and 150 g white sugar
recipe.note: makes about 150 ml, enough for about twenty drinks

cocktail.tagline: You make fun of the world because you haven't given up on it.

reading.epigraph: Bourbon, stirred dry. A four-line poem about San Francisco's 1906 fire ends on whiskey.
whoYouAre: The letter says the changes are "for your convenience". You have a line about it before anyone's finished reading it, and the table groans, then nods, because it's true. People assume you expect the worst of everything.

Here's what they miss. You only notice the gap because you still know how it should be. Under every joke is a picture of something better, and you've never quite given it up. You keep that part quiet. A joke is hard to laugh at; a hope is easy. What wears you out is the pretending: a dinner where everyone agrees to call it fine, and it goes on and on. Further down sits a fear you rarely say: that one day it won't be funny any more.
This matters more than people know. When something's absurd, you make it possible to laugh at it without giving up on it. After your line, everyone breathes out.
yours: After the earthquake and fire of 1906 in San Francisco, several clergymen said the destruction was divine retribution for the city's sins. A city that had just lost so much was told it had deserved it. A whiskey warehouse, A. P. Hotaling's, came through the disaster. People had saved it: its own workers among them, with the fire department and the Navy.

A journalist and poet called Charles K. Field is credited with four lines about it:
*If, as they say, God spanked the town*
*For being over frisky,*
*Why did He burn the churches down*
*And save Hotaling's whiskey?*
I love that it never argues. It asks one question and lets the whiskey answer. It isn't laughing at anyone's faith. It's laughing at the idea that a city in that state had it coming. People were still quoting it a hundred and more years after the fire.

Then his story turns. Two decades after the fire, from 1927 to 1940, Field was on NBC radio with a programme of poetry and inspirational talks, under a made-up name: Cheerio. No press photographs were allowed, and his fee went to charity. The joke is remembered as his. The hope went out under another name. I like to think he wanted it that way.

I think you'd understand him. The jibe and the hope have one root: caring how it turns out. Making fun of the claim stood up for the city. The poetry was the same care, without the joke. Usually only one of the two gets seen.

The cocktail I've made for you starts from a classic that was already on record in the 1800s: a Manhattan made with dry vermouth. Mine is stirred with ice till the mixing glass frosts, then poured, with no ice, into a chilled stemmed glass. Two-thirds of what I pour in is bourbon, because the whiskey is the punchline. Dry vermouth and Angostura, just two dashes, keep it lean. Its lemon is just the oil from the peel: the peel itself comes out. Stirred into all that dryness are one and a half teaspoons of syrup made from a ripe pear, left overnight in sugar. It's in every sip, and nothing on the glass gives it away: a nod to the hope Field sent out under another name, with no face on it. It's a sharp, clean drink with something soft running all through it.

Keep the jokes. Plenty of people get through the week because of them. But once, say the hope out loud, as yourself, before a joke can get there first. Tell someone how you think things could be. It might get laughed at. I'd bet it gets listened to, and I'd love you to find out.
